source.title: Grad Queue : A probabilistic framework to reinforce sparse gradients

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the full paper text, but its result figures are missing; Figure 6 is captioned without plotted values.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates a different gradient method and reports classification performance across batch settings, bearing on whether large-batch performance can improve when the training method changes. The reported results do not establish a training–test generalization gap.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that its gradient-queue methods outperform vanilla optimizers and that more clusters outperform a single cluster for large batches. The underlying Figure 6 is absent, so no numerical values or separate condition-level outcomes can be recovered. The synthetic line example is illustrative and not an evaluated generalization result.
record.test_reason: The study uses the large-batch performance problem to motivate Grad Queue and reports improvements over its base optimizers. The supplied results do not establish held-out performance, equal epoch budgets, or a large-versus-small-batch penalty. They therefore do not test V5 or another claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors propose emphasizing informative gradients using a recent-gradient queue and report improved classification performance over corresponding base optimizers. Their conclusion calls for further work on extracting useful gradients and reducing memory and runtime costs; it does not establish improved held-out generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes a probabilistic gradient-reinforcement method with a finite gradient queue and, for larger batches, clustering; it is not a direct reproduction of the cited large-batch methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that more clusters outperform a single cluster for large batches. They also report experiments with and without momentum and multiple batch sizes, but the missing figures prevent condition-level outcome extraction.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4 reports that GQ-SGDM outperforms SGDM on CIFAR-10 and MNIST, GQ-Adam outperforms Adam on Reuters, and multiple clusters outperform one cluster for large batches. Figure 6's plotted results are unavailable; the text does not identify the evaluation split or training budgets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-queue reinforcement improves reported classification performance relative to the corresponding base optimizer, with clustering providing additional benefits at large batch sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The synthetic line experiment illustrates interference with rare-feature gradients and compares filter learning and loss under SGDM and GQ-SGDM; it supplies no held-out generalization result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reinforcing sparse gradients can improve learning of rare features in the illustrated synthetic task.

record.problems: Figure 6, which contains the reported dataset results, is absent from the supplied text. The text does not identify the plotted accuracy as held-out accuracy, state numerical outcomes, or provide uncertainty estimates. The main comparison therefore cannot establish a training–test gap.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows were extracted. The result statements refer to classification accuracy and performance, but the text does not establish that these are held-out measures; the batch-specific plotted results are unavailable in Figure 6.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed to fit the training data.
Held-out performance of convolutional versus fully connected networks and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning. Reuters uses Adam and the image datasets use SGDM; this is not a controlled comparison between them.
Held-out performance across batch sizes at fixed epoch budgets, and whether an adapted recipe reduces or removes a measured large-batch penalty.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with the training–test generalization gap.
Test accuracy after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The record's designation of V5 as tested is unsupported by the supplied text. Measuring a training–test gap is not necessary to test V5, but held-out batch-size comparisons with a specified epoch budget are necessary here. The unavailable figure results are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not added as missing rows.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test generalization.
Width sweep beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD on held-out performance under stated tuning conditions.

The text discusses and evaluates large batch sizes, but does not state whether the plotted classification accuracy is held-out performance or provide recoverable batch-specific results. Longer training, learning-rate scaling with warmup, normalization changes, and matching small-batch accuracy within a fixed epoch budget are not tested.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting change in test accuracy.
